2 The Study Area and Data
Two data sets will be used in this hands-on exercise, they are:

Hunan county boundary layer. This is a geospatial data set in ESRI shapefile format.
Hunan_2012.csv: This csv file contains selected Hunan’s local development indicators in 2012


2.1 Getting Started
Before we get started, we need to ensure that spdep, sf, tmap and tidyverse packages of R are currently installed.

pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, tmap, tidyverse, knitr)

3 Getting the Data Into R Environment
In this section, you will learn how to bring a geospatial data and its associated attribute table into R environment. The geospatial data is in ESRI shapefile format and the attribute table is in csv fomat.

3.1 Import shapefile into r environment
The code chunk below uses st_read() of sf package to import Hunan shapefile into R. The imported shapefile will be simple features Object of sf.

hunan <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "Hunan")

3.2 Import csv file into r environment
Next, we will import Hunan_2012.csv into R by using read_csv() of readr package. The output is R dataframe class.

hunan2012 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv")



3.3 Performing relational join
The code chunk below will be used to update the attribute table of hunan’s SpatialPolygonsDataFrame with the attribute fields of hunan2012 dataframe. This is performed by using left_join() of dplyr package.

hunan <- left_join(hunan,hunan2012) %>% 
  select(1:4, 7, 15)

4 Visualising Regional Development Indicator
Now, we are going to prepare a basemap and a choropleth map showing the distribution of GDPPC 2012 by using qtm() of tmap package.

basemap <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_text("NAME_3", size=0.3)

gdppc <- qtm(hunan, "GDPPC") +
  tm_layout(
    legend.position = c("left", "bottom"),
    scale = 0.5)
tmap_arrange(basemap, gdppc, asp=1, ncol=2)

5. Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
In this section, we will use poly2nb() of spdep package to compute contiguity weight matrices for the study area. This function builds a neighbours list based on regions with contiguous boundaries. A “queen” argument that takes TRUE or FALSE as options can be passed into the function. If queen = FALSE is not specified, this function will return a list of first order neighbours using the Queen criteria.

5.1 Computing (QUEEN) contiguity based neighbours
The code chunk below is used to compute Queen contiguity weight matrix.

wm_q <- poly2nb(hunan, queen=TRUE)
summary(wm_q)

5.3 Visualising contiguity weights
A connectivity graph takes a point and displays a line to each neighboring point. We are working with polygons at the moment, so we will need to get points in order to make our connectivity graphs. The most typically method for this will be polygon centroids. We will calculate these in the sf package before moving onto the graphs.

Getting Latitude and Longitude of Polygon Centroids
We will need points to associate with each polygon before we can make our connectivity graph. It will be a little more complicated than just running st_centroid on the sf object: us.bound. We need the coordinates in a separate data frame for this to work. To do this we will use a mapping function. The mapping function applies a given function to each element of a vector and returns a vector of the same length. Our input vector will be the geometry column of us.bound. Our function will be st_centroid. We will be using map_dbl variation of map from the purrr package.
To get our longitude values we map the st_centroid function over the geometry column of us.bound and access the longitude value through double bracket notation [[]] and 1. This allows us to get only the longitude, which is the first value in each centroid.

longitude <- map_dbl(hunan$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[1]])

We do the same for latitude with one key difference. We access the second value per each centroid with [[2]].

latitude <- map_dbl(hunan$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[2]])

Now that we have latitude and longitude, we use cbind to put longitude and latitude into the same object.

coords <- cbind(longitude, latitude)

We check the first few observations to see if things are formatted correctly.

text:
6 Computing distance based neighbours
In this section, we will derive distance-based weight matrices by using dnearneigh() of spdep package.
The function identifies neighbours of region points by Euclidean distance with a distance band with lower d1= and upper d2= bounds controlled by the bounds= argument. If unprojected coordinates are used and either specified in the coordinates object x or with x as a two column matrix and longlat=TRUE, great circle distances in km will be calculated assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.

title: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
6.1 Determine the cut-off distance
Firstly, we need to determine the upper limit for distance band by using the steps below:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. The function returns in the units of the coordinates if the coordinates are projected, in km otherwise.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


#coords <- coordinates(hunan)
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.57   38.01   39.07   44.52   61.79 


The summary report shows that the largest first nearest neighbour distance is 61.79 km, so using this as the upper threshold gives certainty that all units will have at least one neighbour.

6.2.1 Plotting fixed distance weight matrix

6.3 Computing adaptive distance weight matrix
One of the characteristics of fixed distance weight matrix is that more densely settled areas (usually the urban areas) tend to have more neighbours and the less densely settled areas (usually the rural counties) tend to have lesser neighbours. Having many neighbours smoothes the neighbour relationship across more neighbours.
It is possible to control the numbers of neighbours directly using k-nearest neighbours, either accepting asymmetric neighbours or imposing symmetry as shown in the code chunk below.

knn6 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k=6))

8. Row-standardised Weights Matrix
Next, we need to assign weights to each neighboring polygon. In our case, each neighboring polygon will be assigned equal weight (style=“W”). This is accomplished by assigning the fraction 1/(#ofneighbors) to each neighboring county then summing the weighted income values. While this is the most intuitive way to summaries the neighbors’ values it has one drawback in that polygons along the edges of the study area will base their lagged values on fewer polygons thus potentially over- or under-estimating the true nature of the spatial autocorrelation in the data. For this example, we’ll stick with the style=“W” option for simplicity’s sake but note that other more robust options are available, notably style=“B”.

rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style="W", zero.policy = TRUE)

9.4 Spatial window sum
The spatial window sum is the counter part of the window average, but without using row-standardized weights.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
text:
The locations of businesses and firms are central to urban development, influencing economic growth, job creation, and the availability of resources and services for residents and other businesses. Strategic locations provide competitive advantages, access to talent and infrastructure, and impact brand image and market positioning, while also shaping the city’s overall character and functionality by fostering specialized districts and facilitating efficient supply chains and employee commutes.

Identify the “where” and “when” of new business entities, revealing clusters, patterns, and trends that are crucial for informed urban planning, resource allocation, and economic development.

We will also visualise the active status for each business type, derived from the entity status description. This will indicate the churn rate in Singapore’s F&B industry and if particular business types are disproportionately facing challenges causing closure.
The following code chunk allows us to examine the possible values in entity_status_description

Next, the following code chunk creates column status which maps “Live Company” and “Live” values as “Active”, and maps all other values as “Not Active”. We then group the data by business type and status to find the total number of businesses of each status type. mutate() is also used to calculate the percentage of each business type of active/not active status, to be used as labels in the plotted bar graph.

# map new status values

  mutate(status = case_when(
    entity_status_description == "Live Company" |  entity_status_description == "Live" |entity_status_description == "Converted To LLP"  ~ "Active",
    TRUE ~ "Not Active"
  ))

# Group data by business type and new status labels

  group_by(TYPE, status) %>% 
  summarise(num_fnb = n())%>%
  mutate(percentage = num_fnb/sum(num_fnb)) # calculate % of active/not active for each business type for labels in graph

# Plot the graph
ggplot(fnb_by_status, aes(fill=status, y=num_fnb, x=TYPE,  label=paste0(round(percentage*100, digits = 1), "%")))+

  y = "Percentage of F&B Businesses"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Active" = "darkolivegreen3", "Not Active" = "darkorange2"))+
  geom_col(position = position_stack()) +
  geom_text(position = position_stack(vjust = .5),  size=3)

Restaurants seem to be slightly more successful in the core central region; while 6% of newly registered cafes and food stalls since January 2024 are no longer active, only 4.5% of newly registered restaurants are no longer active

5.1 Testing for Complete Spatial Randomness

5.1.1 Creating ppp objects
spatstat requires the point event data in ppp object form. The code chunk below uses [as.ppp()] of spatstat package to convert sf objects to ppp format. rjitter() of spatstat package applies a small random displacement to the coordinates of all the points in the ppp object, this avoids duplicate points in the object.

CafesFood StallsRestaurantsCombined business types



cafes_ppp <- as.ppp(cafes_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
cafes_cr_ppp <- cafes_ppp[cr_owin]




foodstalls_ppp <- as.ppp(foodstalls_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
foodstalls_cr_ppp <- foodstalls_ppp[cr_owin]




restaurants_ppp <- as.ppp(restaurants_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
restaurants_cr_ppp <- restaurants_ppp[cr_owin]



For the combined business type ppp object, we want to ensure that the ppp object is typed using the TYPE column in fnb_sf, hence we also create a marks column in the object. factor() is used to create categorical variables from the TYPE column. We then check the final ppp object to ensure we have successfully created a multitype ppp object.

fnb_ppp <- as.ppp(fnb_sf)%>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
fnb_ppp$marks <- factor(fnb_sf$TYPE) 
fnb_cr_ppp <- fnb_ppp[cr_owin]
is.multitype(fnb_cr_ppp)

[1] TRUE







5.1.2 Rescaling ppp objects
The ppp objects are currently using meter as the unit of measurement. The following code chunk converts the unit to measurement to kilometers instead.

cafes_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(cafes_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
foodstalls_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(foodstalls_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
restaurants_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(restaurants_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
fnb_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(fnb_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")



5.1.3 Performing Clark and Evans Test
Next we will perform the Clark and Evans test as a basis to test for ordering of the point event pattern of the location of newly registered businesses. We use the argument method="MonteCarlo" to compute the p-value by comparing R to the results of 999 simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) with the observed number of points.
As we use argument alternative=c('two.sided') our null and alternative hypotheses are as follows:

H0: R=0; The point event pattern is regular or ordered
H1: R =/= 0; the point event pattern is not regular or ordered


CafesFood StallsRestaurants



clarkevans.test(cafes_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  cafes_cr_ppp
R = 0.59678, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided





clarkevans.test(foodstalls_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  foodstalls_cr_ppp
R = 0.4233, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided





clarkevans.test(restaurants_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  restaurants_cr_ppp
R = 0.35005, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided





From the results above, as p-value<0.05 we can reject the null hypothesis at 95% confidence level and conclude that the point pattern of all newly registered F&B businesses since January 2024 are not a regular or ordered point pattern.

  }else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){

      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else {
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }
} else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%

    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%

  }

For all three combinations, significant clustering is consistently observed from distances as low as less than 1km. This means that not only does each F&B business type tend to cluster with other businesses of the same type, they are also likely to be located close to other types of F&B businesses.

6.1 Visualising geographic distribution of F&B businesses by month
Using the lapply() function from base R, we will generate individual maps displaying the point patterns of new F&B businesses as dots and save them into all_maps. The different dot colors correspond with the business type.
Then, we will create an animated gif using tmap_animation() and display the fig using the include_graphics() function from knitr package
We will create an animated GIF from the series of maps stored in the all_maps object using the tmap_animation() function from the tmap package. After generating the GIF, we will display it using the include_graphics() function from the knitr package.






Note



The code for this was modified based on the code in Christover Manafe’s Take Home Exercise 1 visualising a temporal network kernel density estimation map



all_maps <- lapply(1:max(fnb_cr$MONTH_NUM), function(i) {
  
  # filter for the month
  fnb_month <- fnb_cr %>%
    filter(MONTH_NUM==i)
  
  #create title
  title<- paste("Distribution of F&B Businesses at Month ", i)

  # Plot the map for the current month
  map <- tm_shape(cr)+
          tm_polygons() +
        tm_shape(fnb_month)+
          tm_symbols(fill="TYPE", size=0.3) +
    tm_title(title) 
  return(map)
  
})

# creating a gif with all the maps
tmap_animation(all_maps, filename = "img/fnb_animated.gif", 
               width = 1200, height = 1000, dpi = 300, delay=50)


# display the gif
knitr::include_graphics("img/fnb_animated.gif")








Based on this gif, it is clear that there is a consistent hotspot towards the south of the core central region where newly registered F&B businesss are located. Only a handful of new businesses will locate themselves outside of this area each month, with no other particular emerging hotspots.

6.3 Spatio Temporal K function
Finally, we will use analyse whether the point patterns distribution in space and time are random or not. For this, we will use the inhomogenous K-function, which is a second order analysis, The hypotheses are as follows:

H0: The location and timing of event points (newly registered businesses) are independent of all other events.
H1: Location and timing of newly registered businesses are not independent of other new businesses.


6.3.1 Preparing spatio-temporal point process object
The following code chunk extracts the business location coordinates from the respective sf data frames.

cafes_coords <- st_coordinates(cafes_sf)
foodstalls_coords <- st_coordinates(foodstalls_sf)
restaurants_coords <- st_coordinates(restaurants_sf)

Next, we create new data frames by combining the x- and y-coordinates and temporal event (MONTH_NUM). using as.3dpoints() from stpp package then converts the data frame to spatio-temporal object class.

cafes_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = cafes_coords[, 1],  
  y = cafes_coords[, 2],
  t = cafes_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints() 
foodstalls_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = foodstalls_coords[, 1],  
  y = foodstalls_coords[, 2],
  t = foodstalls_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints() 
restaurants_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = restaurants_coords[, 1],  
  y = restaurants_coords[, 2],
  t = restaurants_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints() 

The following code chunks visualises the stpp objects to check correctness of the output.

CafesFood StallsRestaurants



plot(cafes_stpp)











plot(foodstalls_stpp)











plot(restaurants_stpp)













6.3. Computing and Plotting the Spatio-Temporal K Function
Next, STIKhat() of stpp package computes the space-time inhomogenous K function. Finally, plotK() is used to visualise the output.

CafesFood StallsRestaurants



cafes_stik <- STIKhat(cafes_stpp)


plotK(cafes_stik)




foodstalls_stik <- STIKhat(foodstalls_stpp)


plotK(foodstalls_stik)




restaurants_stik <- STIKhat(restaurants_stpp)


plotK(restaurants_stik)




The contours show high values for relatively small values of uu and vv. This suggests that clustering occurs at short spatial and temporal distances, meaning new F&B businesses occur close to each other in both space and time for all business types.
